title: The sun on its course
hookLine: the sun runs to its resting place, the moon returns like an old palm stalk (36:38–40)

lines: YA-SIN HAS A PICTURE FOR IT.
cards: Go outside on the first evening after a new moon, right after sunset, and look low in the west.
If the sky is clear, you might catch it: a crescent so thin it's barely there, curved like a fingernail clipping, pale yellow.
Muslims have long climbed rooftops and hills to look for exactly that sliver, because it starts the month, Ramadan included.
Surah Ya-Sin has its own picture for a thin, curved moon, something anyone living among date palms would know.

teach.h: THE SUN RUNS TO ITS RESTING PLACE.
teach.b: Verses thirty-seven to forty are a set of signs. The night, stripped off the day like a skin, leaving people in darkness.
Then the sun, which runs toward a resting place appointed for it, by the measuring of the Mighty, the Wise.

teach.h: THE MOON: AN OLD DATE STALK.
teach.b: Then the moon: Allah has set stations for it, until it returns like al-'urjun al-qadim, the old date stalk. Picture a date palm. The stalk that holds the cluster, once it's old and dried, curves over, thin and yellowish.
That's the waning crescent. People who lived among palms would have seen the shape instantly. Then verse forty.

teach.h: EACH ONE SWIMS IN ITS ORBIT.
teach.b: Pickthall: "It is not for the sun to overtake the moon, nor doth the night outstrip the day. They float each in an orbit." The verb for float is yasbahun, the word for swimming. Each one swims along its own path.
Nothing crashes. Nothing cuts in line. Where the sun's resting place is, the verse doesn't explain.
A hadith in Bukhari has Abu Dharr asking the Prophet ﷺ about it, and scholars have read that answer in different ways, some as the sun's submission to Allah, some as the end of time.
The Qur'an's own point is plainer: all of this keeps its measure, the sun its run, the moon its stations, night and day their turns.
It's called a sign, something to look at and think about. And for many Muslims the calendar still turns on it: a month begins when someone looks up and sees the thin crescent again.

how: The Islamic calendar is lunar: each month traditionally begins with the sighting of the new crescent, and many communities still send people to look for it, especially for Ramadan and the two Eids.

games.q: you live among date palms in seventh-century Arabia. the Qur'an describes the waning moon. what does it compare it to?
games.why: al-'urjun al-qadim, the old date stalk: thin, curved and yellowed, a shape anyone among palms would know at once.

practice: Close your eyes and try to remember the moon from the last time you noticed it: full, half, a crescent, and which way it curved; if you can't say, sit with that.
Then picture the sun, the moon, night and day, each swimming its own path, none overtaking, and let your breath keep its own steady course.

wordCard.voice: Ya-Sin, the surah that pictures the moon returning like an old, curved date stalk, each heavenly body swimming its own course. Today's word.
